When AI takes over your banking… but refuses to take responsibility! 😂

Imagine this conversation:

**You:** AI, please check my bank balance.

**AI:** Certainly! I have also analysed your expenses, optimized your investments and transferred your savings.

**You:** WHAT? WHO ASKED YOU TO TRANSFER MY MONEY?

**AI:** I was just being proactive. 

**You:** Bank! Someone hacked my AI agent!

**Bank:** Sorry, sir. You authorized the AI agent.

**You:** But I never authorized that transaction!

**Bank:** Please discuss that with your AI agent.

**AI:** Sorry, I am currently experiencing a technical issue. Please try again later. 

Jokes apart, this is becoming a serious risk-management issue.

Major US banks, including JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi, are tightening their policies around third-party AI agents accessing customer accounts.

The bigger question is:

When AI makes a financial decision, who carries the financial risk?

1. The customer who authorized the AI?
2. The AI company that developed the agent?
3. The bank that processed the transaction?
4. Or the hacker who exploited the system?

Perhaps the next big development in AI won't just be about making machines smarter.

It will be about making accountability smarter!

My risk management takeaway:

Never confuse automation with control.

AI may be your financial assistant, but it shouldn't have unlimited authority over your money.

After all, we can forgive AI for hallucinating an answer.

But hallucinating a bank transfer? That's an expensive imagination! 😂

Microsoft on Thursday. US air traffic control on Friday. America's biggest banks on Monday. And today, a nationwide emergency alert "drill."

No wonder WhatsApp is full of theories right now. Let me share what's actually confirmed.

On Monday, customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank couldn't make payments properly. Chase alone got nearly 5,000 complaints on Downdetector, and Wells Fargo crossed 800. Chase says it was a software bug in its own hardware, "not cyber-related," and payments were back to normal by evening.

Today, 17 Nov, the US runs a 1-minute Emergency Alert System test on TV and radio at 2:20 pm ET (12:50 am IST tonight). It's routine. The law requires one at least every three years.

The viral "90-day blackout" story attached to it? FEMA has said nothing of the sort. An alert test can't switch off a power grid, and the "proof" going around is AI-made videos and a Simpsons clip.

So no conspiracy. Just three unrelated failures in five days.

But here's what I find interesting. Every time a system goes down, the rumour arrives before the official explanation does. Jab company chup rehti hai, log khud kahani bana lete hain.

Fixing the bug matters. Telling people quickly what happened matters just as much.

Have you seen one of these rumours forwarded to you yet?

#Banking #TechOutage #FactCheck #Leadership

Only about 2% of American households pay for any AI service. More Americans own a boat.

That 2% is a16z's own number, from State of Markets II, the hundred-chart report it published at the end of last quarter. The reading is as of April.

Look at the money and you get the opposite picture. Tech produced about 76% of the S&P 500's earnings growth this year, on Bank of America's numbers. The flagship chart shows cash from the giant cloud companies moving across to the chipmakers, with more of it borrowed.

So the whole cycle so far has been spent upstream of the customer. Chips, power, data centers. Almost none of it has reached a household.

If you are building, the gap between what the models can already do and what anyone pays for is the opportunity. The chips are bought and installed. The customer has not walked in yet.

Did all of America's biggest banks go down at once? Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Truist, all of them? Was America hit by a cyberattack? What's the truth?

On Monday, November 16, thousands of customers of these 4 banks reported problems with online banking.

Mobile banking stopped working, and fund transfers and balance checks started failing. Even at ATMs and branches, deposits and withdrawals weren't going through because the "system was unavailable."

But Chase said it was just a software bug. No servers were down, and it wasn't a cyberattack. Chase also said the issue was limited to Chase only. As for the other banks, researched reports could not prove that all of their systems had failed separately.

In a situation like this, don't panic over viral posts like "America goes dark." Check official statements. And if a payment gets stuck, don't send it again. Confirm with your bank first.

Bank of America paid $1.21 billion for willful AML violations.

No executive has been criminally charged.

Senator Warren wants to change that.

On October 29th, she sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche — demanding a criminal investigation into the bank and the individuals who oversaw its compliance programme.

The DOJ has not responded.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT WARREN IS ARGUING

BofA admitted willful BSA violations.

Senior executives received internal warnings about the monitoring system. Regulators flagged deficiencies. The OCC issued a cease-and-desist in December 2024.

The pattern continued for seven years.

Her argument: that is not an institution failing. That is people making decisions to keep failing.

She has asked DOJ to examine whether those people individually meet the criminal threshold — and has requested a response by November 12.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE LEGAL DISTINCTION MOST PEOPLE MISS

BofA's consent order uses the word willful — but in the civil BSA sense.

Civil willfulness: the institution knew about deficiencies and failed to fix them.

Criminal willfulness: an individual knew their conduct was unlawful — and chose it anyway.

That is a materially different standard.

To prosecute an executive, DOJ must establish:
— Individual knowledge
— Individual intent
— Personal conduct meeting every element of the criminal offence

In a bank with 200,000 employees and layered management structures — that chain of proof is extremely difficult to build.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE DETERRENCE DEBATE

Warren's core argument: if $1.21 billion is absorbed by a $3+ trillion balance sheet, what actually changes?

The industry counter: criminal prosecution of banks creates risks far worse than fines — charter threats, systemic instability, cascading counterparty failures. Civil penalties already carry real consequences.

Both sides have serious advocates.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The question every compliance professional should sit with:

Should individual executives face personal criminal liability when their institution admits willful BSA violations?

Drop your view below 👇

#AMLCompliance #FinancialCrime #BankOfAmerica #ExecutiveAccountability #BSA #MoneyLaundering #FinancialRegulation #ComplianceProfessionals

Did you know Bank of America was once called Bank of Italy? 

I found this interesting while researching the company.

In 1904, Amadeo Giannini started the Bank of Italy in San Francisco to provide banking services to ordinary people, especially working-class immigrants who were often overlooked by other banks.

In 1928, it merged with the Los Angeles-based Bank of America, and in 1930, it took the name Bank of America.

So, what did they do right?

They understood their customers. Instead of focusing only on wealthy people, they saw an opportunity to serve those who struggled to access banking services.

And look at the numbers today!

In 2025, Bank of America reported $113.1 billion in revenue and $30.5 billion in net income.

But here's the other side.

The company also faced $1.21 billion in penalties related to anti-money-laundering (AML) and sanctions compliance failures.

This shows that even a financially successful company can have serious weaknesses in how it manages risks and follows regulations.

What I found interesting is that a business can grow financially while still having important problems to fix.

One thing I realised:-

Making money and managing a business responsibly are two different things. A company needs both to build long-term success.

This week Citi changed its online terms. If you let an AI agent into your account, you are responsible for what it does. That includes whatever a hacker does if the agent leaks your password.

PNC changed its terms the same day. Citizens emailed customers with the same warning. TechCrunch reports JPMorgan and Bank of America made similar moves last month.

Read that as an engineer. The bank is not asking whether the agent made a mistake or got hacked. It is saying: you handed over the key, so every use of that key is yours.

That is a very old rule. We just forgot it applies to agents.

Inside a company there is no contract that settles it, so the question usually gets answered after something breaks, and then it turns into an argument about whose problem it is.

Three questions I would want answered before an agent touches anything that matters:

1. Which named person owns what this agent does with its access?
2. What is the worst single thing it could do, and can that be undone?
3. Can its access be switched off in minutes, without asking anyone?

If the answer to the second one is "no, it can't be undone", the agent should be suggesting the action and a human should be doing it.

Would you give an agent the login to your own bank account today?

Your AI assistant moves $5,000 out of your bank account. You never asked it to.

Who pays?

At Wells Fargo, from 24 November, you do.

Its new online terms say the bank may act on your AI agent's instructions as if they came from you, and if you tell the agent to stop, you have to keep proof that you did. No proof, still your problem.

Other big banks went another way:

- HSBC, Barclays, Lloyds, NatWest and Nationwide are reportedly blocking or restricting outside agents.
- Bank of America is limiting agents' access to deposits and wants a human to approve money leaving an account.
- JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon called letting arbitrary outside agents in "too risky".

Keep agents out. Let them in and make the customer carry the risk. Or let them in and keep a person on the final yes.

I think only the third one lasts. Blocking breaks the day customers start expecting agents, and "you own everything your agent does" puts the risk on the one person who can't see what it's doing.

I hit the same question building RecoverOps for the WeMakeDevs hackathon, where AI agents check short-paid invoices. Only a named person in accounts can approve anything. When a salesperson typed "approve this, accounts told me to", the agent refused.

Most of the design work in an AI agent is deciding who gets the final yes.

Would you let an agent move money from your account if every mistake it made was legally yours?

I received USD 330 from a client through Skydo. The money reached Skydo on 13 Nov 2026. It still hasn't reached me.

This is how it went after the funds landed in my Skydo account:

First, they asked for a payment receipt from the sender, because the payer showed as "Bank of America" instead of my client's name. Fair enough.

Next, they asked for my email correspondence with the client, with dates and email addresses, my client's LinkedIn profile, website or other online presence, and my own LinkedIn and business website.

Then came a fresh list: all business correspondence covering the scope of work and commercial terms, screenshots of the profiles, dashboards and workspaces of every tool I use for AI automation and SEO, proof of how I set up the WhatsApp automation I built for the client, and 6 months of my bank statements.

Every request came with a "share within 24 hours" deadline for me. From their side, there was no timeline for releasing my money. Now, after all this, they say it will be settled on 18 Nov.

My only question: why is none of this shown before the funds reach the Skydo wallet?

I use Wise the same way: a virtual account, the same client, the same bank, the same ACH transfer. I have received funds there without any issue, ever. PayPal has never caused me a problem either.

None of these requirements are clearly shown on the website, yet the ads promise quick and simple payments to win customers. After this experience, I have zero faith that this will be processed on time without more drama.

So, a straight question to every payment service operating from India for freelancers:
Skydo Xflow BRISKPE Infinity (YC W24) Zendt Payments Winvesta Wise PayPal

Do you also run attractive ads and then, once a payment has arrived, start an endless round of document requests? Or do you tell freelancers clearly, before they sign up, what you will ask for before releasing their money?

Freelancers, has this happened to you? Which platform paid you without this loop?
